q: By what local name is "slash and burn" agriculture known in Jharkhand?
e: In Jharkhand, slash and burn (primitive subsistence) agriculture is locally called "Kuruwa".

q: Which one of the following is a rabi crop?
e: Wheat, barley, peas, gram and mustard are major rabi crops sown in winter (October–December).

q: Which of the following is an example of a kharif crop?
e: Rice, maize, jowar, bajra, tur, moong, urad, cotton, jute and groundnut are major kharif crops.

q: Crops like watermelon, muskmelon and cucumber grown in the short summer season between rabi and kharif belong to which cropping season?
e: The short summer cropping season between the rabi and kharif seasons is known as the Zaid season.

q: Which fibre crop is known as the "golden fibre" in India? [JAC PYQ]
e: Jute is known as the golden fibre; West Bengal is its leading producer.

q: What is India’s rank in the world in the production of rice after China?
e: India is the second largest producer of rice in the world after China.

q: Which is a leading tea producing state in India?
e: Major tea-producing states are Assam, hills of Darjeeling and Jalpaiguri in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Kerala.

q: Which is the leading rubber-producing state in India?
e: Rubber is mainly grown in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andaman & Nicobar Islands, with Kerala leading.

q: What is the rearing of silkworms for the production of silk fibre known as?
e: Rearing of silkworms for the production of silk fibre is known as sericulture.

q: Which one of the following is a leguminous crop that helps restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air?
e: All pulses except arhar are leguminous crops that help in restoring soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air.

q: Who initiated the "Bhoodan-Gramdan" movement?
e: Vinoba Bhave initiated the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement, also known as the Blood-less Revolution.

q: What is the type of commercial farming where a single crop is grown on a large area (like tea, coffee, rubber) called?
e: Plantation is a type of commercial farming where a single crop is grown on a large area; it acts as an interface of agriculture and industry.

q: Which crop grows well in drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan plateau?
e: Cotton grows well in drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan plateau.

q: Which state of India is famous for cultivating both rubber and bananas as important plantation/horticultural crops?
e: Kerala is a leading producer of both rubber and bananas in India.

q: Where is Intensive Subsistence Farming primarily practised?
o: Areas of high population pressure on land
e: Intensive subsistence farming is practised in areas of high population pressure on land using high biochemical inputs and irrigation.

q: What is "slash and burn" agriculture called in north-eastern states like Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland?
e: It is known as "Jhumming" in north-eastern states like Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland.

q: Which three are the important millets grown in India?
e: Jowar, bajra and ragi are the important millets grown in India, known for very high nutritional value.

q: Which country is the largest producer as well as consumer of pulses in the world?
e: India is the largest producer as well as the consumer of pulses in the world, which are the major source of protein in a vegetarian diet.

q: India is the second largest producer of sugarcane only after which country?
e: India is the second largest producer of sugarcane only after Brazil.

q: Which variety of coffee initially brought from Yemen is produced in India and known worldwide for its good quality?
e: The Arabica variety initially brought from Yemen is produced in India; its cultivation was initially introduced on the Baba Budan Hills.

q: Even today, Indian coffee cultivation is largely confined to Nilgiri across which three southern states?
e: Even today, coffee cultivation in India is confined to Nilgiri in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

q: Which three crops of paddy are grown in a single year in Assam, West Bengal and Odisha?
e: In states like Assam, West Bengal and Odisha, three crops of paddy are grown in a year: Aus, Aman and Boro.

q: Which millet is very rich in iron, calcium, other micro nutrients and roughage?
e: Ragi is very rich in iron, calcium, other micro nutrients and roughage.

q: Which group of states represents major cotton producers in India?
o: Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh
e: Major cotton-producing states are Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, AP, Telangana, TN, Punjab, Haryana and UP.

q: Which reform based on package technology brought significant agricultural improvements in India during the 1960s and 1970s?
e: In the 1960s and 1970s, the Green Revolution based on package technology and the White Revolution (Operation Flood) were major strategies to improve agriculture.

q: What does KCC stand for among institutional schemes introduced for Indian farmers?
e: Kissan Credit Card (KCC) and Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS) were introduced by the Government of India for the benefit of farmers.

q: Which one of the following is NOT an oilseed?
e: Groundnut, mustard, coconut, sesamum, soyabean, castor seeds, cotton seeds, linseed and sunflower are oilseeds; tur (arhar) is a pulse.

q: What is "slash and burn" agriculture known as in Mexico and Central America?
e: Slash and burn is known as "Milpa" in Mexico and Central America, "Conuco" in Venezuela, "Roca" in Brazil, "Ladang" in Indonesia, and "Ray" in Vietnam.

q: On which hills was coffee cultivation initially introduced in India?
e: Coffee cultivation in India was initially introduced on the Baba Budan Hills in Karnataka.

q: Which crop takes almost a full year to grow?
e: Sugarcane takes almost a year to grow.

q: Which state is the largest producer of Jute (Golden Fibre) in India? [JAC PYQ]
e: West Bengal is the leading producer of jute in India, followed by Bihar, Assam, Odisha and Meghalaya.

q: Which one of the following describes a system of agriculture where a single crop is grown on a large area? [JAC PYQ]
e: Plantation agriculture is a type of commercial farming in which a single crop is grown on a large area.

q: Which one of the following is a rabi crop? [JAC PYQ]
e: Gram is a rabi crop sown in winter, whereas rice and cotton are kharif crops.

q: Which one of the following is a leguminous crop? [JAC PYQ]
e: Pulses (except arhar) are leguminous crops that fix atmospheric nitrogen to restore soil fertility.

q: Tea cultivation is an example of which type of agriculture? [JAC PYQ]
e: Tea, coffee, rubber, sugarcane and banana are important plantation crops in India.

q: Which is the staple food crop of a majority of the people in India?
e: Rice is the staple food crop of a majority of the people in India.

q: How many frost-free days does cotton require to grow well?
e: Cotton requires high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine for its growth.

q: What rainfall and temperature conditions are required for growing rubber?
o: Less than 50 cm rain and below 10°C
Moist and humid climate with rainfall more than 200 cm and temperature above 25°C
e: Rubber is an equatorial crop requiring moist and humid climate with rainfall of more than 200 cm and temperature above 25°C.

q: What temperature and annual rainfall conditions are required for rice cultivation?
o: High temperature above 25°C, high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm
e: Rice is a kharif crop requiring high temperature (above 25°C), high humidity and annual rainfall above 100 cm.

q: What seasonal climate and annual rainfall does wheat cultivation require?
o: Cool growing season, bright sunshine at ripening and 50 to 75 cm of evenly distributed annual rainfall
e: Wheat requires a cool growing season and a bright sunshine at the time of ripening, with 50 to 75 cm of annual rainfall evenly distributed over the growing season.

q: What temperature and annual rainfall are ideal for sugarcane cultivation?
o: Hot and humid climate with 21°C–27°C and annual rainfall between 75 cm and 100 cm
e: Sugarcane grows well in hot and humid climate with a temperature of 21°C to 27°C and an annual rainfall between 75 cm and 100 cm.

q: At Pochampalli in Andhra Pradesh (now Telangana), who offered 80 acres of land to be distributed among 80 landless villagers when Vinoba Bhave spoke?
e: Suddenly, Shri Ram Chandra Reddy stood up and offered 80 acres of land to be distributed among 80 land-less villagers; this act was known as "Bhoodan".

q: In India, Sesamum (til) is grown in which contrasting seasons in North and South India?
o: Kharif crop in north and rabi crop in south India
Rabi in north and kharif in south India
e: Sesamum is a kharif crop in north and rabi crop in south India; castor seed is grown both as rabi and kharif crop.

q: Which pulse does NOT help restore soil fertility via nitrogen fixation unlike other pulses?
e: Per NCERT, being leguminous crops, all pulses except arhar help in restoring soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air.

q: Which crop is used both as food and fodder, and though mainly a kharif crop is also grown in rabi season in Bihar?
e: Maize is used both as food and fodder; it is a kharif crop requiring 21°C–27°C and grows well in old alluvial soil, though in states like Bihar it is grown in rabi season also.

q: Groundnut is primarily which seasonal crop, accounting for about half of major oilseeds produced in India?
e: Groundnut is a kharif crop and accounts for about half of the major oilseeds produced in the country (Gujarat is largest producer).

q: What phenomenon during winter months helps in the success of rabi crops in northern and north-western India?
o: Availability of precipitation during winter months due to western temperate cyclones
e: Availability of precipitation during winter months due to the western temperate cyclones helps in the success of rabi crops.

q: What was the main focus of India’s First Five Year Plan regarding agriculture?
e: Collectivisation, consolidation of holdings, cooperation and abolition of zamindari were given priority; "Land reform" was the main focus of the First Five Year Plan.

q: What are the local names of "slash and burn" agriculture in Madhya Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh respectively?
e: In India this primitive form of cultivation is called "Bewar" or "Dahiya" in Madhya Pradesh and "Podu" or "Penda" in Andhra Pradesh.

q: Where is tea processed in India so as to restore its freshness?
e: Tea is processed within the tea garden to restore its freshness.

q: What is Jowar’s rank among important food crops of India in area/production, and which state is its major producer?
o: Third most important food crop with respect to area and production — Maharashtra major producer
e: Jowar is the third most important food crop with respect to area and production; Maharashtra was its major producer alongside Karnataka, AP and MP.

q: On which soils does Bajra grow well, and which state is among its major producers?
o: Sandy soils and shallow black soil — Rajasthan major producer
e: Bajra grows well on sandy soils and shallow black soil; major Bajra producing states are Rajasthan, UP, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Haryana.

q: Nagpur and Cherrapunjee are famous in India for which horticulture fruit?
e: India is famous for oranges of Nagpur and Cherrapunjee (Meghalaya), mangoes of Maharashtra/AP/UP/WB, pineapples of Meghalaya, and litchi/guava of UP and Bihar.

q: Which institutional protections were introduced during the 1980s and 1990s comprehensive land development programme?
o: Crop insurance against drought/flood/cyclone/fire/disease, Grameen banks/cooperatives for low interest loans, KCC, PAIS and MSP
e: Provision for crop insurance, Grameen banks and cooperatives for low-interest loans, KCC, PAIS, weather bulletins and MSP were key steps of the 1980s–1990s reforms.

q: While rice is a subsistence crop in Odisha, what is it in Haryana and Punjab?
e: The degree of commercialisation of agriculture varies from one region to another; for example, rice is a commercial crop in Haryana and Punjab, but in Odisha, it is a subsistence crop.

q: In what soil and terrain conditions does jute grow best?
o: Well-drained fertile soils in the flood plains where soils are renewed every year
e: Jute grows well on well-drained fertile soils in the flood plains where soils are renewed every year; high temperature is required during the time of growth.

q: Different oilseeds are grown covering approximately what percentage of the total cropped area of India?
e: Different oil seeds are grown covering approximately 12 per cent of the total cropped area of the country.

q: Why is "organic farming" much in vogue today according to NCERT?
o: Because it is practised without factory made chemicals such as fertilisers and pesticides, hence it does not affect environment in a negative manner
e: Organic farming is much in vogue today because it is practised without factory made chemicals such as fertilisers and pesticides, so it does not affect the environment negatively.

q: Cotton is which type of seasonal crop and how long does it take to mature?
o: Kharif crop — requires 6 to 8 months to mature
e: Cotton is a kharif crop and requires 6 to 8 months to mature; India is believed to be the original home of the cotton plant.

q: Which are the two important wheat-growing zones in India?
o: The Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and black soil region of the Deccan
e: There are two important wheat-growing zones in the country—the Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and black soil region of the Deccan.

q:
Match the local name of "slash and burn" cultivation with its Indian state/region:
A. Jharkhand — 1. Podu / Penda
B. Andhra Pradesh — 2. Kuruwa
C. Western Ghats — 3. Dahiya / Bewar
D. Madhya Pradesh — 4. Kumari
e: Jharkhand = Kuruwa (A-2); Andhra Pradesh = Podu/Penda (B-1); Western Ghats = Kumari (C-4); MP = Dahiya/Bewar (D-3).

q:
Match the global name of shifting cultivation correctly:
1. Brazil — A. Ladang
2. Indonesia — B. Milpa
3. Mexico — C. Roca
e: Brazil = Roca (1-C); Indonesia = Ladang (2-A); Mexico = Milpa (3-B).

q: A farmer has a small uneconomical landholding due to the right of inheritance dividing land across generations, yet applies high doses of biochemical inputs and irrigation to extract maximum output. Identify this farming type:
e: In intensive subsistence farming, though the right of inheritance renders landholdings uneconomical, farmers take maximum output using high biochemical inputs and irrigation.

q: A tropical/subtropical crop requires hot humid climate (21°C–27°C), 75–100 cm rainfall, manual labour from sowing to harvesting, grows on varied soils, and India is its 2nd largest producer after Brazil. Identify it:
e: These exact conditions describe sugarcane, the main source of sugar, gur (jaggery), khandsari and molasses.

q: How has it become possible to grow rice in areas of less rainfall such as Punjab, Haryana, western UP and parts of Rajasthan?
o: Development of dense network of canal irrigation and tubewells
e: Development of dense network of canal irrigation and tubewells have made it possible to grow rice in areas of less rainfall such as Punjab, Haryana and western UP.

q: In India, which region experienced the most notable success of the Green Revolution primarily in wheat and paddy?
o: Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan
e: The success of the Green Revolution in Punjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan has been an important factor in the growth of crops like wheat.

q: A farmer prepares black soil fields in a climate offering 210 frost-free days and bright sunshine for a 6–8 month kharif cycle. Which crop is he cultivating?
e: Cotton is a kharif crop grown in black soil needing 210 frost-free days, bright sunshine, and 6–8 months to mature.

q: Why do farmers grow pulses (except arhar) in rotation with cereal crops?
o: Leguminous pulses restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air
Pulses grow only in desert dunes
e: Being leguminous crops, pulses (except arhar) fix nitrogen from the air to restore soil fertility, making them mostly grown in rotation with other crops.

q: Among cotton, jute, hemp and natural silk, what makes natural silk uniquely different in its agricultural origin?
o: The first three are derived from crops grown in the soil, whereas natural silk is obtained from cocoons of silkworms fed on green leaves (especially mulberry)
The first three come from animals
e: Cotton, jute and hemp are derived from crops grown in soil, whereas silk is obtained from cocoons of silkworms fed on green leaves especially mulberry (sericulture).

q: Which golden fibre crop of India is losing its market to synthetic fibres and packing materials, particularly nylon, due to its high cost?
e: Due to its high cost, jute is losing market to synthetic fibres and packing materials, particularly nylon.

q:
Arrange India’s annual cropping cycle chronologically starting from April:
1. Harvesting of rabi crops
2. Cultivation of Zaid summer crops (watermelon, cucumber)
3. Sowing of kharif crops with onset of monsoon
4. Harvesting kharif (Sept–Oct) and sowing winter rabi crops
e: April–June: Rabi harvesting (1) and Zaid summer crops (2); Monsoon onset: Kharif sowing (3); Sept–Dec: Kharif harvest followed by Rabi sowing (4).

q: What climatic conditions distinguish ideal tea cultivation?
o: Warm and moist frost-free climate all through the year with frequent showers evenly distributed over the year
e: Tea bushes require a warm and moist frost-free climate all through the year; frequent showers evenly distributed ensure continuous growth of tender leaves.

q: How does the "right of inheritance" adversely affect Indian agriculture?
o: It leads to division of land among successive generations, rendering land-holding size small and uneconomical
It merges all villages into one farm
e: Though the right of inheritance leads to division of land among successive generations rendering land-holding size uneconomical, farmers continue to take maximum output from the limited land.

q: Which industrial raw-material crop from Kerala/Tamil Nadu is widely used in manufacturing auto tyres, tubes and footwear?
e: Natural rubber is an important industrial raw material grown mainly in Kerala, TN, Karnataka and Andaman & Nicobar.

q: According to NCERT, although Maize is predominantly a kharif crop, in which state is it grown in rabi season also?
e: NCERT notes that maize is a kharif crop, but in some states like Bihar maize is grown in rabi season also.

q: Which pair of states leads in Groundnut (Gujarat) and Cotton/Jowar (Maharashtra/Deccan)?
e: Gujarat is the largest producer of groundnut, and both Gujarat and Maharashtra are leading cotton producers.

q:
Match the Indian fruit crop with its noted growing region:
1. Nagpur — A. Litchi and Guava
2. UP and Bihar — B. Oranges
3. Meghalaya — C. Apples and Walnuts
4. J&K and Himachal Pradesh — D. Pineapples
e: Nagpur = Oranges (1-B); UP/Bihar = Litchi/Guava (2-A); Meghalaya = Pineapples (3-D); J&K/HP = Apples/Walnuts (4-C).

q: Why does the Government announce Minimum Support Price (MSP), remunerative and procurement prices for important crops?
o: To check the exploitation of farmers by speculators and middlemen
e: Government announces MSP, remunerative and procurement prices for important crops to check the exploitation of farmers by speculators and middlemen.

q: Which characteristic distinguishes Plantation Agriculture from Primitive Subsistence Farming in terms of capital and labour?
o: Plantation uses capital intensive inputs with migrant labourers, whereas primitive subsistence relies on family/community labour and primitive tools
e: Plantation is done using capital intensive inputs with migrant labourers producing raw materials for industries; primitive subsistence uses hoe, dao, digging sticks and family/community labour.

q: Why was the Bhoodan-Gramdan movement initiated by Vinoba Bhave termed the "Blood-less Revolution"?
o: Because land and entire villages were voluntarily donated for distribution among landless villagers peacefully without bloodshed (some also due to fear of land ceiling act)
e: It peacefully transferred land to the landless without violence/bloodshed (though some landowners feared the land ceiling act), earning the name Blood-less Revolution.

q: Which soil pairing matches Maize (old alluvial) and Cotton (black soil) correctly?
o: Maize: old alluvial soil; Cotton: black cotton soil
Both grow only in saline marsh
e: Maize grows well in old alluvial soil, while cotton grows well in drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan plateau.

q: Which statement accurately describes Ragi’s growing conditions and states in India?
o: It grows only in flooded deltas
It is a crop of dry regions growing well on red, black, sandy, loamy and shallow black soils (Karnataka, TN, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, etc.)
e: Ragi is a crop of dry regions and grows well on red, black, sandy, loamy and shallow black soils; major producers include Karnataka, TN, HP, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Jharkhand and Arunachal Pradesh.

q: Besides being edible cooking mediums, oilseeds in India are also used as raw materials in manufacturing which industrial goods?
e: Most oilseeds are edible and used as cooking mediums, while some are also used as raw material in the production of soap, cosmetics and ointments.

q: Why is tea cultivation specifically described as a "labour-intensive industry"?
o: Because it requires abundant, cheap and skilled labour for plucking tender leaves and processing within the tea garden
e: Tea is a labour-intensive industry requiring abundant, cheap and skilled labour; it is processed within the tea garden to restore its freshness.

q: How did agricultural reform priorities shift from the 1960s–70s to the 1980s–90s in India?
o: 1960s–70s focused on package tech (Green/White Revolutions) which stayed regionally concentrated, so 1980s–90s launched a comprehensive institutional and technical land development programme (crop insurance, Grameen banks, KCC, MSP)
e: Green/White revolutions of 1960s–70s led to concentration of development in selected areas, prompting a comprehensive land development programme combining institutional and technical reforms in the 1980s–90s.

q: Identify the INCORRECT pairing of crop and required temperature conditions:
e: Wheat is a rabi crop requiring a cool growing season and bright sunshine at ripening, not 35°C–45°C with frost.

q: Contrast paddy cultivation in Assam/WB/Odisha with Punjab/Haryana:
o: Assam, WB and Odisha grow three paddy crops a year (Aus, Aman, Boro) due to humid climate, while Punjab/Haryana grow rice commercially via canals and tubewells
Punjab grows Aus, Aman and Boro
e: Assam, WB and Odisha grow three paddy crops (Aus, Aman, Boro), whereas Punjab and Haryana rely on canals and tubewells to grow rice commercially.

q: What are the local names for shifting cultivation in Manipur and Bastar (Chhattisgarh) / Andaman & Nicobar Islands respectively?
e: It is called "Pamlou" in Manipur and "Dipa" in Bastar district of Chhattisgarh and in Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

q: Linseed and mustard are oilseed crops grown in which season in India?
e: Linseed and mustard are rabi crops; groundnut is kharif; sesamum is kharif in north and rabi in south; castor is both.

q: In which group are ALL listed crops predominantly grown in the Kharif season?
e: Paddy, maize, cotton, jute and groundnut are all key kharif crops. Wheat, gram, barley, mustard and peas are rabi crops, while watermelon is zaid.

q:
Read the passage: "Primitive subsistence agriculture is practised on small patches of land with the help of primitive tools like hoe, dao and digging sticks, and family/community labour. This type of farming depends upon monsoon, natural fertility of the soil and suitability of other environmental conditions to the crops grown. It is a slash and burn agriculture. Farmers clear a patch of land and produce cereals and other food crops to sustain their family. When the soil fertility decreases, the farmers shift and clear a fresh patch of land for cultivation."

What factors does primitive subsistence farming primarily depend upon?
o: Monsoon, natural fertility of soil and suitability of other environmental conditions
e: As stated in the passage, primitive subsistence farming depends upon monsoon, natural soil fertility and other environmental conditions.

q: When do farmers in this "slash and burn" system shift and clear a fresh patch of land?
o: When the soil fertility of the earlier patch decreases
e: When the soil fertility decreases, farmers shift and clear a fresh patch of land allowing nature to replenish fertility.

q: Why is land productivity low in this type of farming?
o: Because the farmer does not use fertilisers or other modern inputs
e: Land productivity in this type of agriculture is low as the farmer does not use fertilisers or other modern inputs.

q: What are the local names for this farming system in Jharkhand and North-eastern states (Assam/Meghalaya/Mizoram/Nagaland) respectively?
e: It is known as Kuruwa in Jharkhand and Jhumming in Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland.

q: What is the primary goal of production in this agricultural system as indicated in the passage?
o: Producing cereals and other food crops to sustain the family
e: Farmers produce cereals and food crops primarily to sustain their family rather than commercial profit.

q:
Read the passage: "Cotton is a kharif crop and requires 6 to 8 months to mature. India is believed to be the original home of the cotton plant. Cotton is one of the main raw materials for cotton textile industry. Cotton grows well in drier parts of the black cotton soil of the Deccan plateau. It requires high temperature, light rainfall or irrigation, 210 frost-free days and bright sun-shine for its growth."

India is believed to be the original home of which plant?
e: As noted in the passage, India is believed to be the original home of the cotton plant.

q: Cotton belongs to which cropping season and takes how long to mature?
e: Cotton is a kharif crop and takes 6 to 8 months to mature.

q: Which soil of the drier Deccan plateau region is ideal for cotton production?
e: Black cotton soil (regur soil) of the drier Deccan plateau is ideal for cotton growth.

q: How many frost-free days are required for cotton to grow well?
e: Cotton needs 210 frost-free days along with high temperature, light rainfall/irrigation and bright sunshine.

q: Which combination of states represents leading cotton-producing states of India?
o: Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya and Sikkim
Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka and Telangana
e: Maharashtra, Gujarat, MP, Karnataka, AP, Telangana, TN, Punjab, Haryana and UP are India’s major cotton-producing states.

q:
Consider the following statements about Indian agriculture:
I. Ganga-Satluj plains in the north-west and black soil region of the Deccan are India’s two major wheat zones.
II. India is the second largest producer of sugarcane in the world after Brazil.
III. All pulses including Arhar help restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen.
Which are correct?
e: Statements I and II are true. Statement III is incorrect because NCERT explicitly notes "all pulses EXCEPT arhar" restore soil fertility by fixing nitrogen.

q:
Match each oilseed with its Indian cropping season classification:
A. Groundnut — 1. Both Rabi and Kharif
B. Mustard and Linseed — 2. Kharif in North, Rabi in South
C. Sesamum (Til) — 3. Rabi crop
D. Castor seed — 4. Primarily Kharif crop
e: Groundnut = Kharif (A-4); Mustard/Linseed = Rabi (B-3); Sesamum = Kharif North/Rabi South (C-2); Castor = Both (D-1).

q: Which one of the following statements about India’s cropping seasons is INCORRECT?
o: Rabi crops are sown Oct–Dec and harvested Apr–June
Kharif crops are sown with onset of monsoon and harvested Sept–Oct
Aus, Aman and Boro in Assam, WB and Odisha are three varieties of maize
Watermelon, muskmelon and cucumber are grown during the Zaid season
e: Aus, Aman and Boro are three crops of **paddy (rice)** grown in a year in Assam, WB and Odisha—not varieties of maize.

q: Which option correctly pairs each millet with one of its prominent producing states from NCERT?
o: Jowar: Maharashtra; Bajra: Rajasthan; Ragi: Karnataka
Jowar: Assam; Bajra: Kerala; Ragi: Punjab
Jowar: Kashmir; Bajra: Bengal; Ragi: Goa
Jowar: Manipur; Bajra: Mizoram; Ragi: Tripura
e: Per NCERT, Jowar is majorly produced in Maharashtra, Bajra in Rajasthan, and Ragi in Karnataka.

q:
Arrange these agricultural reforms in India chronologically (earliest to latest):
1. Comprehensive land development programme (crop insurance, Grameen banks, KCC, PAIS)
2. Abolition of zamindari and First Five Year Plan focus on land reform
3. Green Revolution (package technology) and White Revolution
e: Land reforms / 1st Five Year Plan (1950s) → Green & White Revolutions (1960s–70s) → Comprehensive institutional & technical programme incl. crop insurance, KCC, PAIS (1980s–90s).

q: Identify the crop sequence matching these exact annual rainfall requirements: (>100 cm), (75–100 cm), and (50–75 cm):
e: NCERT specs: Rice (>100 cm), Sugarcane (75–100 cm), Wheat (50–75 cm evenly distributed).

q: Which two factors together drove high rabi wheat output in Punjab, Haryana and western UP?
o: Winter rainfall from western temperate cyclones + Green Revolution package technology (irrigation and HYV seeds)
e: Winter precipitation from western temperate cyclones and the Green Revolution’s success in Punjab, Haryana and western UP together fuelled rabi output.

q: Which statement regarding Rubber cultivation in India is INCORRECT?
o: It is an equatorial crop also grown in tropical/sub-tropical areas under special conditions
It requires moist/humid climate with >200 cm rain and >25°C temperature
In India it is primarily cultivated across the arid plains of Punjab and Rajasthan
It is an important industrial raw material
e: Rubber grows in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andaman & Nicobar and Garo hills of Meghalaya—not in dry Punjab or Rajasthan.

q:
Match the shifting cultivation term with its region:
1. Podu — A. Odisha
2. Koman/Bringa — B. Vietnam
3. Ray — C. Venezuela
4. Conuco — D. Andhra Pradesh
e: Podu = Andhra Pradesh (1-D); Koman/Bringa = Odisha (2-A); Ray = Vietnam (3-B); Conuco = Venezuela (4-C).

q: Which contrast accurately distinguishes India’s tea-growing regions from its coffee-growing regions?
o: Major tea hubs lie in Assam and North Bengal (Darjeeling/Jalpaiguri) alongside TN/Kerala, whereas coffee cultivation remains confined mainly to Nilgiri across Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu
e: Tea thrives prominently in Assam, Darjeeling/Jalpaiguri (WB), TN, Kerala, plus HP/Uttarakhand/NE states, whereas Indian coffee cultivation is confined mainly to Nilgiri across Karnataka, Kerala and TN.

q: Why must institutional reforms (like rural banks, cooperatives, KCC, crop insurance, consolidation) accompany technological reforms (HYV, irrigation)?
o: Because modern technological inputs require capital, and without affordable institutional credit, consolidation and crop insurance, small farmers cannot adopt them safely
e: Smallholders require affordable credit, consolidation of fragmented holdings and insurance protection to adopt expensive modern inputs without falling into debt traps.

q: Spot the INCORRECT comparison among Primitive Subsistence, Intensive Subsistence, and Plantation farming:
o: Primitive subsistence: small patches, primitive tools, monsoon dependence
Intensive subsistence: high population pressure, high biochemical inputs and irrigation
Plantation: single crop over large area, interface of agriculture and industry
Plantation: growing diverse crops solely for household consumption without capital
e: Plantation is commercial, capital-intensive monoculture for industries/markets, NOT zero-capital multi-crop household subsistence.

q: A farmer sows Crop X in November and harvests in April; then sows Crop Y with the monsoon onset in June and harvests in September. Which valid pair of crops could (X, Y) be?
o: (X = Wheat or Gram, Y = Jowar or Bajra)
e: November sowing (rabi) fits wheat or gram (X), while June monsoon sowing (kharif) fits jowar or bajra (Y).

q: Which group consists EXCLUSIVELY of "non-food" crops as classified in NCERT Geography Chapter 4?
e: NCERT classifies sugarcane, oilseeds, tea and coffee under "Food Crops other than Grains", while Rubber, Cotton and Jute are "Non-Food Crops".

q: Which statement accurately reflects India’s position in Horticulture crops?
o: India produces about 13% of the world’s vegetables and is an important producer of pea, cauliflower, onion, cabbage, tomato, brinjal and potato
e: India produces about 13 per cent of the world’s vegetables and is an important producer of pea, cauliflower, onion, cabbage, tomato, brinjal and potato, alongside tropical & temperate fruits.

q: Which soil characteristic is essential for tea plantation?
o: Deep and fertile well-drained soil, rich in humus and organic matter
e: The tea plant grows well in tropical/sub-tropical climates endowed with deep and fertile well-drained soil, rich in humus and organic matter.

q: What broader geographic trend is evident in sugarcane production across India alongside northern states like UP and Bihar?
o: Being both a tropical and sub-tropical crop, alongside UP and Bihar, southern states like Maharashtra, Karnataka, TN, AP and Telangana are major producers
Sugarcane grows only on Himalayan peaks
e: Sugarcane is a tropical as well as a subtropical crop; major producers are UP, Maharashtra, Karnataka, TN, AP, Telangana, Bihar, Punjab and Haryana.

q: Identify the INCORRECT crop–fact pair:
o: Rice: India is 2nd largest producer after China
Sugarcane: India is 2nd largest producer after Brazil
Cotton: India is believed to be the original home of cotton
Coffee: India alone produces 80% of total world coffee
e: Indian coffee (Arabica) is world-renowned for quality, not quantity (Brazil leads globally; India does not produce 80%).

q: Which regional pair for shifting cultivation names in India is INCORRECT?
e: In Jharkhand it is called **Kuruwa**, whereas **Pamlou** is used in Manipur.

q: "Operation Flood" (White Revolution) introduced in the 1960s–70s was aimed at transforming which agricultural/allied sector?
e: The White Revolution (Operation Flood) was aimed at boosting milk production alongside the Green Revolution.

q: The use of higher doses of modern inputs such as High Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides in order to obtain higher productivity defines:
e: The main characteristic of commercial farming is the use of higher doses of modern inputs (HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, insecticides and pesticides) to obtain higher productivity.

q: Which sequence accurately narrates how the Bhoodan movement began at Pochampalli?
o: During Vinoba Bhave’s padyatra, landless villagers demanded land → Vinoba assured to speak to government → Shri Ram Chandra Reddy stood up and offered 80 acres to 80 landless villagers
e: During Vinoba Bhave’s padyatra at Pochampalli (AP), poor landless villagers demanded land; when he promised to talk to govt, Shri Ram Chandra Reddy spontaneously offered 80 acres for 80 landless families.

q: Which list accurately represents the products derived from sugarcane as noted in NCERT?
e: Sugarcane is the main source of sugar, gur (jaggery), khandsari and molasses.

q: Which state–crop pairing is INCORRECT according to NCERT Geography Chapter 4?
o: Grapes — Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Maharashtra
Bananas — Kerala, Mizoram, Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu
Groundnut — Gujarat, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu
e: Jute is grown in the fertile flood plains of West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, Odisha and Meghalaya, not in Rajasthan or Ladakh.

q: What physical relief feature is especially vital for both tea and coffee plantations compared to jute cultivation?
o: Tea and coffee thrive on well-drained hill slopes so water does not stagnate, whereas jute grows in flat alluvial flood plains
All three grow on sandy beaches
e: Tea and coffee require well-drained hill slopes to prevent waterlogging, whereas jute flourishes in flat flood plains where soil is renewed annually.

q: Which pair of 1980s–90s reforms specifically addressed farmers’ risk of natural calamities and accidental vulnerability?
o: Crop insurance against drought/flood/cyclone/fire/disease and Personal Accident Insurance Scheme (PAIS)
e: Crop insurance against drought, flood, cyclone, fire and disease alongside PAIS and KCC directly targeted farmer vulnerability and risk.

q: Why do both Pulses and Millets (Jowar, Bajra, Ragi) hold exceptional nutritional significance in Indian agriculture?
o: Pulses are the major source of protein in a vegetarian diet, while millets (especially ragi) have very high nutritional value rich in iron, calcium, micronutrients and roughage
e: Pulses provide essential vegetarian protein while coarse grains/millets like ragi are packed with iron, calcium, micronutrients and roughage.

q: What distinguished "Gramdan" from "Bhoodan" in Vinoba Bhave’s movement?
o: Bhoodan involved donating plots of land to landless villagers, while in Gramdan some zamindars and owners of many villages offered to distribute some villages among the landless
e: Offering plots of land (like 80 acres at Pochampalli) was Bhoodan; later, zamindars owning entire villages offered to distribute whole villages among the landless, known as Gramdan.

q: Why was "Consolidation of holdings" (Chakbandi) prioritised after Independence in India?
o: To merge fragmented, small uneconomical landholdings caused by the right of inheritance into viable plots fit for modern farming
To plant forests on every farm
To confiscate all land for malls
To move all villagers to cities
e: Because the right of inheritance fragmented holdings into tiny uneconomical plots, consolidation of holdings was prioritised to enable viable modern farming.

q: Which summary statement accurately reflects the overall significance of agriculture in India as introduced in NCERT?
o: India is an agriculturally important country where two-thirds of its population is engaged in agricultural activities; it is a primary activity producing most food and raw material for industries
e: Two-thirds of India’s population is engaged in agricultural activities; it is a primary activity producing most of our food and raw materials for various industries.
